L0102.text: You type a question into a little lit box.
L0102.spoken: You type a question... into a little lit box.

L0103.text: Something that is not a person writes back, word by word.
L0103.spoken: Something that is not a person writes back... word by word.

L0104.text: By one count, at least seven hundred million people use such machines every week.
L0104.spoken: By one count, at least seven hundred million people use such machines every week.

L0105.text: Yet nobody ever wrote one a rulebook.
L0105.spoken: Yet nobody ever wrote one a rulebook.

L0107.text: When ChatGPT launched, late in 2022, its makers admitted a flaw.
L0107.spoken: When Chat G P T launched, late in twenty twenty-two, its makers admitted a flaw.

L0108.text: In their words, it “sometimes writes plausible-sounding but incorrect or nonsensical answers.”
L0108.spoken: In their words, it "sometimes writes plausible-sounding but incorrect or nonsensical answers."

L0109.text: Put that in the case file.
L0109.spoken: Put that... in the case file.

L0110.text: On the case board, three suspects. Rules. Knowledge. And learning.
L0110.spoken: On the case board, three suspects. Rules. Knowledge. And learning.

L0114.text: We go back to the war years, to a lamp in Chicago.
L0114.spoken: We go back to the war years... to a lamp in Chicago.

L0202.text: A shy teenager, Walter Pitts, found a home with a doctor, Warren McCulloch.
L0202.spoken: A shy teenager, Walter Pitts, found a home with a doctor, Warren McCullock.

L0203.text: In 1943 they described a nerve cell as a switch. All, or nothing.
L0203.spoken: In nineteen forty-three they described a nerve cell as a switch. All, or nothing.

L0204.text: Enough signals at once, and it fired. Wire such cells into a network, a neural network, and you had logic.
L0204.spoken: Enough signals at once, and it fired. Wire such cells into a network, a neural network, and you had logic.

L0209.text: We light the first candle. Each belief gets one, burning as long as it was held. This one: the brain is a logic machine.
L0209.spoken: We light the first candle. Each belief gets one, burning as long as it was held. This one: the brain is a logic machine.

L0210.text: Ralph Gerard, at its rim, argued the brain was more dial than switch.
L0210.spoken: Ralph Gerard, at its rim, argued the brain was more dial than switch.

L0211.text: Donald Hebb guessed: when one cell helps fire another, their link grows.
L0211.spoken: Donald Hebb guessed: when one cell helps fire another, their link grows.

L0212.text: Alan Turing, in 1950, proposed something stranger: not to program a grown-up mind, but to educate a child machine.
L0212.spoken: Alan Turing, in nineteen fifty, proposed something stranger: not to program a grown-up mind, but to educate a child machine.

L0215.text: By 1956 the field had a name: artificial intelligence.
L0215.spoken: By nineteen fifty-six the field had a name: artificial intelligence.

L0215b.text: Marvin Minsky, who had built a learning machine himself, soon turned to symbols and rules: our first suspect.
L0215b.spoken: Marvin Minsky, who had built a learning machine himself, soon turned to symbols and rules: our first suspect.

L0216.text: A young engineer, Bernard Widrow, fell for the dream of building an artificial brain, for good. His machines learned by sliding downhill, toward less wrong.
L0216.spoken: A young engineer, Bernard Widrow, fell for the dream of building an artificial brain, for good. His machines learned by sliding downhill, toward less wrong.

L0218.text: A 1959 study of the frog's eye found the eye itself already sorting the world, picking out features before the brain saw a thing.
L0218.spoken: A nineteen fifty-nine study of the frog's eye found the eye itself already sorting the world, picking out features before the brain saw a thing.

L0219.text: The logic-machine candle burned sixteen years.
L0219.spoken: The logic-machine candle burned sixteen years.

L0220.text: The paper that put it out, for Pitts at least, had his own name on it.
L0220.spoken: The paper that put it out, for Pitts at least, had his own name on it.

L0302.text: Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron, a program on a borrowed computer, learns in fifty tries to sort cards marked left or right.
L0302.spoken: Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron, a program on a borrowed computer, learns in fifty tries to sort cards marked left or right.

L0303.text: Newspapers said the Navy expected it to “walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.”
L0303.spoken: Newspapers said the Navy expected it to "walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence."

L0304.text: In fairness, the Navy, the press and Rosenblatt all fed the hype.
L0304.spoken: In fairness, the Navy, the press and Rosenblatt all fed the hype.

L0305.text: A second candle: a machine that learns will soon see, talk and think.
L0305.spoken: A second candle: a machine that learns will soon see, talk and think.

L0306.text: At its rim stood Marvin Minsky, who doubted such nets could tell whether a shape was in one piece, or two.
L0306.spoken: At its rim stood Marvin Minsky, who doubted such nets could tell whether a shape was in one piece, or two.

L0307.text: In Buffalo, Rosenblatt built it as a machine: an eye, random wires, and motor-driven knobs. Each knob sets how strongly one wire counts: its weight.
L0307.spoken: In Buffalo, Rosenblatt built it as a machine: an eye, random wires, and motor-driven knobs. Each knob sets how strongly one wire counts: its weight.

L0308.text: When it was wrong, only the knobs of lit wires turned, a little, toward the answer.
L0308.spoken: When it was wrong, only the knobs of lit wires turned, a little, toward the answer.

L0309.text: You could hear it learn. I love that.
L0309.spoken: You could hear it learn. I love that.

L0310.text: A theorem promised the rule would find a dividing line.
L0310.spoken: A theorem promised the rule would find a dividing line.

L0312.text: A magazine asked what use it was. “At the moment, none whatever,” Dr. Rosenblatt said cheerfully. And what could it never do? “Love,” he said. “Hope. Despair.”
L0312.spoken: A magazine asked what use it was. "At the moment, none whatever," Doctor Rosenblatt said cheerfully. And what could it never do? "Love," he said. "Hope. Despair."

L0318.text: In his 1961 book: “Linguistic capability, related to perceptual experience, is of the essence.” Put that in the file.
L0318.spoken: In his nineteen sixty-one book: "Linguistic capability, related to perceptual experience, is of the essence." Put that in the file.

L0319.text: By the mid-sixties, most of the other groups had moved on. The learning-machine candle burned about seven years.
L0319.spoken: By the mid-sixties, most of the other groups had moved on. The learning-machine candle burned about seven years.

L0320.text: Then two men wrote a book about what a single layer of knobs could never do.
L0320.spoken: Then two men wrote a book about what a single layer of knobs could never do.

L0401.text: The book’s simplest puzzle: exclusive-or. Light up if one input is on, not both. On a square, the lit cases sit at opposite corners.
L0401.spoken: The book's simplest puzzle: exclusive-or. Light up if one input is on, not both. On a square, the lit cases sit at opposite corners.

L0402.text: No straight cut can separate them.
L0402.spoken: No straight cut can separate them.

L0403.text: Two cuts can: a hidden layer, cells between input and answer. Nobody in the mainstream knew how to train one.
L0403.spoken: Two cuts can: a hidden layer, cells between input and answer. Nobody in the mainstream knew how to train one.

L0404.text: In 1969, Minsky and Papert’s book proved what one layer cannot do.
L0404.spoken: In nineteen sixty-nine, Minsky and Papert's book proved what one layer cannot do.

L0405.text: For many layers, it offered only what it called “our intuitive judgment that the extension is sterile”, while naming it a problem worth settling. A third candle: many layers are a dead end.
L0405.spoken: For many layers, it offered only what it called "our intuitive judgment that the extension is sterile", while naming it a problem worth settling. A third candle: many layers are a dead end.

L0406.text: That year, Congress tied defence-funded research to military uses, and the snow began: the first AI winter.
L0406.spoken: That year, Congress tied defence-funded research to military uses, and the snow began: the first A.I. winter.

L0408.text: That May, Walter Pitts died alone. McCulloch followed four months later.
L0408.spoken: That May, Walter Pitts died alone. McCullock followed four months later.

L0409.text: In 1971, on his forty-third birthday, Frank Rosenblatt drowned while sailing.
L0409.spoken: In nineteen seventy-one, on his forty-third birthday, Frank Rosenblatt drowned while sailing.

L0410.text: In 1973, James Lighthill’s report for Britain blamed “the combinatorial explosion”. It struck rules far more than nets. Yet British funding fell for almost a decade.
L0410.spoken: In nineteen seventy-three, James Lighthill's report for Britain blamed "the combinatorial explosion". It struck rules far more than nets. Yet British funding fell for almost a decade.

L0411.text: One book's fault? Historians still argue; there were several blows.
L0411.spoken: One book's fault? Historians still argue; there were several blows.

L0412.text: Still, a few windows stayed lit. In Helsinki, the next clue sat unnoticed in a student's thesis about rounding errors.
L0412.spoken: Still, a few windows stayed lit. In Helsinki, the next clue sat unnoticed in a student's thesis about rounding errors.

L0415.text: Sussex, 1976. A young Geoffrey Hinton takes his place, far from the flame.
L0415.spoken: Sussex, nineteen seventy-six. A young Geoffrey Hinton takes his place, far from the flame.

L0416.text: He would spend much of the next thirty-six years near the edge of the light.
L0416.spoken: He would spend much of the next thirty-six years near the edge of the light.

L0501.text: Versailles, 1981. John Hopfield presents a network.
L0501.spoken: Versailles, nineteen eighty-one. John Hopfield presents a network.

L0524.text: Give it half a memory, and it rolls downhill, like a ball, until the whole memory returns.
L0524.spoken: Give it half a memory, and it rolls downhill, like a ball, until the whole memory returns.

L0505.text: At the sterile candle’s rim, all the while, stood Geoffrey Hinton.
L0505.spoken: At the sterile candle's rim, all the while, stood Geoffrey Hinton.

L0505b.text: With two colleagues, he built a net that settles as it cools.
L0505b.spoken: With two colleagues, he built a net that settles as it cools.

L0507.text: October 1986: a paper by David Rumelhart, Hinton and Ronald Williams. Light flows up through layers of lanterns, our nerve cells. The answer is checked against the right one; the error glows.
L0507.spoken: October, nineteen eighty-six: a paper by David Rumelhart, Hinton and Ronald Williams. Light flows up through layers of lanterns, our nerve cells. The answer is checked against the right one; the error glows.

L0508.text: Then a messenger, back-propagation, runs back down, lantern by lantern, tugging each knob by its share of the blame.
L0508.spoken: Then a messenger, back-propagation, runs back down, lantern by lantern, tugging each knob by its share of the blame.

L0509.text: Again and again, until our exclusive-or puzzle is solved. By itself.
L0509.spoken: Again and again, until our exclusive-or puzzle is solved. By itself.

L0521.text: The sterile extension, it turns out, was not. That candle burned seventeen years.
L0521.spoken: The sterile extension, it turns out, was not. That candle burned seventeen years.

L0510.text: Each tug, a step downhill toward less error, in fog.
L0510.spoken: Each tug, a step downhill toward less error, in fog.

L0511.text: Who invented the messenger? Several people, separately, that Helsinki student among them. The 1986 paper made it stick.
L0511.spoken: Who invented the messenger? Several people, separately, that Helsinki student among them. The nineteen eighty-six paper made it stick.

L0512.text: Hinton later wrote: “I have never claimed that I invented backpropagation.”
L0512.spoken: Hinton later wrote: "I have never claimed that I invented backpropagation."

L0513.text: Since about 1980, our second suspect had its own candle: intelligence is knowledge, typed in by hand.
L0513.spoken: Since about nineteen eighty, our second suspect had its own candle: intelligence is knowledge, typed in by hand.

L0514.text: One expert system, built from experts' rules, was rated above Stanford specialists, yet never went into routine use.
L0514.spoken: One expert system, built from experts' rules, was rated above Stanford specialists, yet never went into routine use.

L0515.text: Doug Lenat's team lit its own candle: common sense, by hand. They wrote that AI could draw “practically nothing” from raw text.
L0515.spoken: Doug Lenat's team lit its own candle: common sense, by hand. They wrote that A.I. could draw "practically nothing" from raw text.

L0522a.text: In 1984, at a panel, insiders warned of a coming winter.
L0522a.spoken: In nineteen eighty-four, at a panel, insiders warned of a coming winter.

L0522.text: By 1987 the special machines for these programs stopped selling: a second winter. The knowledge candle burned about seven years.
L0522.spoken: By nineteen eighty-seven the special machines for these programs stopped selling: a second winter. The knowledge candle burned about seven years.

L0523.text: Two critics asked: can a net that says John loves the girl always say the girl loves John? Still argued.
L0523.spoken: Two critics asked: can a net that says John loves the girl always say the girl loves John? Still argued.

L0519.text: The messenger worked. Within a decade, most of the field had stopped listening.
L0519.spoken: The messenger worked. Within a decade, most of the field had stopped listening.

L0601.text: 1989, Bell Labs: Yann LeCun's network learns to read handwritten ZIP codes from Buffalo's mail.
L0601.spoken: Nineteen eighty-nine, Bell Labs: Yann Le Cun's network learns to read handwritten zip codes from Buffalo's mail.

L0603.text: By 1998, a descendant “reads several million checks per day.”
L0603.spoken: By nineteen ninety-eight, a descendant "reads several million checks per day."

L0604.text: A winter, then, of prestige, not of use.
L0604.spoken: A winter, then, of prestige, not of use.

L0605.text: The rivals were good: classical machine learning. In speech and translation, statistics learned from data beat hand-written rules. Forests of decision trees voted.
L0605.spoken: The rivals were good: classical machine learning. In speech and translation, statistics learned from data beat hand-written rules. Forests of decision trees voted.

L0606.text: The favourite, Vladimir Vapnik's support vector machine, finds the widest street between two crowds.
L0606.spoken: The favourite, Vladimir Vapnik's support vector machine, finds the widest street between two crowds.

L0607.text: Its landscape is one clean bowl, with a proof you'll reach the bottom.
L0607.spoken: Its landscape is one clean bowl, with a proof you'll reach the bottom.

L0608.text: The candle of the age: neural nets are fiddly, they stall in the fog, and they're beaten anyway.
L0608.spoken: The candle of the age: neural nets are fiddly, they stall in the fog, and they're beaten anyway.

L0609.text: At its rim, a few stubborn holdouts, among them Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio. “We couldn't get our papers published,” LeCun said.
L0609.spoken: At its rim, a few stubborn holdouts, among them Geoffrey Hinton, Yann Le Cun and Yoshua Bengio. "We couldn't get our papers published," Le Cun said.

L0610.text: In 1995, at Bell Labs, two colleagues signed a pair of bets, a fancy dinner each. Larry Jackel bet that by 2000 we would understand why big neural nets work. Vladimir Vapnik bet that by 2005 “no one in his right mind” would use nets like those.
L0610.spoken: In nineteen ninety-five, at Bell Labs, two colleagues signed a pair of bets, a fancy dinner each. Larry Jackel bet that by two thousand we would understand why big neural nets work. Vladimir Vapnik bet that by two thousand and five "no one in his right mind" would use nets like those.

L0612.text: So who paid for dinner? Keep that question.
L0612.spoken: So who paid for dinner? Keep that question.

L0613.text: Through many layers, or a long sentence read word by word, the messenger fades like a whisper.
L0613.spoken: Through many layers, or a long sentence read word by word, the messenger fades like a whisper.

L0614.text: In 1997, Hochreiter and Schmidhuber’s protected pipe carried it over a thousand steps.
L0614.spoken: In nineteen ninety-seven, Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's protected pipe carried it over a thousand steps.

L0615.text: The chess crown, promised for 1968, came twenty-nine years late, won by search, not by a neural network. A point for Rules.
L0615.spoken: The chess crown, promised for nineteen sixty-eight, came twenty-nine years late, won by search, not by a neural network. A point for Rules.

L0701.text: Who paid for dinner? Both men. By 2000, no one could yet explain why big nets work. By 2005, people were still using them. Each man lost one bet.
L0701.spoken: Who paid for dinner? Both men. By two thousand, no one could yet explain why big nets work. By two thousand and five, people were still using them. Each man lost one bet.

L0702.text: In 2006, a new candle: before any right answers, warm up a deep net, many layers tall, one layer at a time, each rebuilding its own input.
L0702.spoken: In two thousand and six, a new candle: before any right answers, warm up a deep net, many layers tall, one layer at a time, each rebuilding its own input.

L0703.text: Fast computers, big data, good starting weights: “All three conditions are now satisfied,” Hinton and a student wrote. Nearly right: the third turned out optional.
L0703.spoken: Fast computers, big data, good starting weights: "all three conditions are now satisfied," Hinton and a student wrote. Nearly right: the third turned out optional.

L0704.text: Accomplice one: data. Fei-Fei Li recalls colleagues telling her to do something more useful. Labelling her millions of pictures by hand would have taken nineteen years.
L0704.spoken: Accomplice one: data. Fay-Fay Lee recalls colleagues telling her to do something more useful. Labelling her millions of pictures by hand would have taken nineteen years.

L0705.text: A crowd did it: almost fifty thousand people.
L0705.spoken: A crowd did it: almost fifty thousand people.

L0712.text: It became ImageNet, and a yearly contest: a thousand categories.
L0712.spoken: It became Image Net, and a yearly contest: a thousand categories.

L0706.text: Accomplice two: fire. Graphics chips, built for games, trained networks up to seventy times faster.
L0706.spoken: Accomplice two: fire. Graphics chips, built for games, trained networks up to seventy times faster.

L0707.text: In 2010, plain back-propagation on one graphics chip set a record on handwritten digits, no warm-up.
L0707.spoken: In twenty ten, plain back-propagation on one graphics chip set a record on handwritten digits, no warm-up.

L0710.text: The warm-up candle guttered; nobody knows exactly when.
L0710.spoken: The warm-up candle guttered; nobody knows exactly when.

L0802.text: Since about 1999, the belief: to see, a machine needs patterns designed by experts, by hand. Even allowed five guesses a picture, the best program missed more than one in four.
L0802.spoken: Since about nineteen ninety-nine, the belief: to see, a machine needs patterns designed by experts, by hand. Even allowed five guesses a picture, the best program missed more than one in four.

L0803.text: In Hinton's Toronto lab, Ilya Sutskever, sure deep nets would keep improving with more data, talked Alex Krizhevsky into trying.
L0803.spoken: In Hinton's Toronto lab, Ilya Soots-kever, sure deep nets would keep improving with more data, talked Alex Kri-zhevsky into trying.

L0805.text: A photograph is a grid of lights, each light a number. In colour, three numbers: red, green, blue. One small photo: a hundred and fifty thousand numbers.
L0805.spoken: A photograph is a grid of lights, each light a number. In colour, three numbers: red, green, blue. One small photo: a hundred and fifty thousand numbers.

L0806.text: Hold a pierced tin stencil over the picture, a light behind it.
L0806.spoken: Hold a pierced tin stencil over the picture, a light behind it.

L0807.text: Each of its nine holes weighs the light beneath it. Add them up. Below zero counts as zero.
L0807.spoken: Each of its nine holes weighs the light beneath it. Add them up. Below zero counts as zero.

L0808.text: Over an edge, the sum is nearly four: a bright spot. Now the lovely part: slide the same stencil everywhere. A convolution.
L0808.spoken: Over an edge, the sum is nearly four: a bright spot. Now the lovely part: slide the same stencil everywhere. A convolution.

L0809.text: Ninety-six stencils at the bottom; four more layers above, each stencilling the one below: edges, then textures, parts, things.
L0809.spoken: Ninety-six stencils at the bottom; four more layers above, each stencilling the one below: edges, then textures, parts, things.

L0810.text: Then two great halls, where every lantern sees everything, and a last hall of a thousand lanterns, one per answer.
L0810.spoken: Then two great halls, where every lantern sees everything, and a last hall of a thousand lanterns, one per answer.

L0811.text: Nobody cut these stencils. They began as noise, like television snow.
L0811.spoken: Nobody cut these stencils. They began as noise, like television snow.

L0812.text: The messenger from 1986 cut them, nudge by nudge.
L0812.spoken: The messenger from nineteen eighty-six cut them, nudge by nudge.

L0813.text: Older nets squashed strong signals flat. The below-zero rule is a weir: strong signals pass undimmed, so the messenger's tug stays strong. The net learned six times faster, in the team's test.
L0813.spoken: Older nets squashed strong signals flat. The below-zero rule is a weir: strong signals pass undimmed, so the messenger's tug stays strong. The net learned six times faster, in the team's test.

L0815.text: Sixty million weights, yet each label, one name in a thousand, is worth about ten yes-or-no answers. Twelve million answers in all. It could memorise the photos, not learn to see.
L0815.spoken: Sixty million weights, yet each label, one name in a thousand, is worth about ten yes-or-no answers. Twelve million answers in all. It could memorise the photos, not learn to see.

L0816.text: So they cropped and mirrored the pictures.
L0816.spoken: So they cropped and mirrored the pictures.

L0830.text: In the great halls, they snuffed a random half each time, so no lantern could count on another. Like a team where anyone might be missing, each had to know the work.
L0830.spoken: In the great halls, they snuffed a random half each time, so no lantern could count on another. Like a team where anyone might be missing, each had to know the work.

L0817.text: The network ran on two graphics chips, GPUs, half the stencils on each.
L0817.spoken: The network ran on two graphics chips, G P Us, half the stencils on each.

L0818.text: Nobody told the two halves how to divide the work. One cut edges, mostly colour-blind; the other, colour. Every time.
L0818.spoken: Nobody told the two halves how to divide the work. One cut edges, mostly colour-blind; the other, colour. Every time.

L0819.text: Then five or six days downhill in fog, the stride shortened three times, by hand.
L0819.spoken: Then five or six days downhill in fog, the stride shortened three times, by hand.

L0821.text: A bad back kept Hinton from flying. Yann LeCun stood at the rear of a packed room.
L0821.spoken: A bad back kept Hinton from flying. Yann Le Cun stood at the rear of a packed room.

L0822.text: Second place missed twenty-six point two percent. Alex's network, AlexNet, fifteen point three.
L0822.spoken: Second place missed twenty-six point two percent. Alex's network, Alex Net, fifteen point three.

L0834.text: Fair credit: that was seven networks voting; one alone, nearer eighteen.
L0834.spoken: Fair credit: that was seven networks voting; one alone, nearer eighteen.

L0825.text: And a Swiss lab's nets had already won contests on graphics chips.
L0825.spoken: And a Swiss lab's nets had already won contests on graphics chips.

L0826.text: The hand-cut stencil candle burned thirteen years. It went out in one: at the next contest, all top five teams used such nets.
L0826.spoken: The hand-cut stencil candle burned thirteen years. It went out in one: at the next contest, all top five teams used such nets.

L0831.text: Beside it, the fiddly-nets candle went out too, after ten to fifteen years, field by field.
L0831.spoken: Beside it, the fiddly-nets candle went out too, after ten to fifteen years, field by field.

L0832.text: Why choose the fog? The rivals' clean bowl sat on stencils cut by hand. In the fog, given data and fire, the net cut its own, many layers deep: deep learning.
L0832.spoken: Why choose the fog? The rivals' clean bowl sat on stencils cut by hand. In the fog, given data and fire, the net cut its own, many layers deep: deep learning.

L0832b.text: And Hinton? Thirty-six years near the edge of the light. Now, it found him.
L0832b.spoken: And Hinton? Thirty-six years near the edge of the light. Now, it found him.

L0827.text: Our results, the paper said, can be improved simply by waiting for faster GPUs and bigger datasets to become available.
L0827.spoken: Our results, the paper said, can be improved simply by waiting for faster G P Us and bigger datasets to become available.

L0901.text: A new candle, then a creed: deep learning works on everything.
L0901.spoken: A new candle, then a creed: deep learning works on everything.

L0902.text: December 2012. By one reporter’s account, Hinton auctioned his three-person company, halted the bidding at forty-four million dollars, and chose Google.
L0902.spoken: December, twenty twelve. By one reporter's account, Hinton auctioned his three-person company, halted the bidding at forty-four million dollars, and chose Google.

L0905.text: In 2014, a Go programmer gave machines “maybe ten years” to beat a professional. It took under two.
L0905.spoken: In twenty fourteen, a Go programmer gave machines "maybe ten years" to beat a professional. It took under two.

L0905b.text: DeepMind's AlphaGo learned from human games, then from itself, rewarded for wins.
L0905b.spoken: Deep Mind's Alpha Go learned from human games, then from itself, rewarded for wins.

L0906.text: Seoul, 2016. AlphaGo played move thirty-seven, a one-in-ten-thousand move.
L0906.spoken: Seoul, twenty sixteen. Alpha Go played move thirty-seven, a one-in-ten-thousand move.

L0907.text: Then Lee Sedol found a move just as rare, and won the match’s only human game.
L0907.spoken: Then Lee Seh-dol found a move just as rare, and won the match's only human game.

L0909.text: Months before Seoul, OpenAI was founded, co-chaired by Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Human-level AI, it said, “could benefit society”, or “damage society if built or used incorrectly.”
L0909.spoken: Months before Seoul, Open A.I. was founded, co-chaired by Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Human-level A.I., it said, "could benefit society", or "damage society if built or used incorrectly."

L0909b.text: Its backers committed a billion dollars.
L0909b.spoken: Its backers committed a billion dollars.

L0910.text: At the rim, doubters. Changes too small to see could fool these nets. Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru found commercial face software misread the gender of darker-skinned women far more often than of lighter-skinned men. The candle burned on, and still does, argued over.
L0910.spoken: At the rim, doubters. Changes too small to see could fool these nets. Joy Boo-oh-lam-weenee and Timnit Gebru found commercial face software misread the gender of darker-skinned women far more often than of lighter-skinned men. The candle burned on, and still does, argued over.

L1002.text: Another candle, lit in 1997 with that protected pipe: language must be read in order.
L1002.spoken: Another candle, lit in nineteen ninety-seven with that protected pipe: language must be read in order.

L1005.text: In 2014, translating machines squeezed a whole sentence into one list of numbers: a bottleneck. So they learned to look back at every word: attention.
L1005.spoken: In twenty fourteen, translating machines squeezed a whole sentence into one list of numbers: a bottleneck. So they learned to look back at every word: attention.

L1006.text: Over lunch at Google in 2016, Jakob Uszkoreit suggested keeping only the attention.
L1006.spoken: Over lunch at Google in twenty sixteen, Jakob Oosh-ko-rite suggested keeping only the attention.

L1007.text: Colleagues doubted it. One later called his doubt “the biggest incorrect prediction of my life.”
L1007.spoken: Colleagues doubted it. One later called his doubt "the biggest incorrect prediction of my life."

L1009.text: Drop the word-by-word reader, keep the attention: every word looks at every other, all at once. The Transformer.
L1009.spoken: Drop the word-by-word reader, keep the attention: every word looks at every other, all at once. The Transformer.

L1024.text: Its title: Attention Is All You Need. From English to German, it out-translated every rival after half a day's training.
L1024.spoken: Its title: Attention Is All You Need. From English to German, it out-translated every rival after half a day's training.

L1010.text: Each word arrives as a learned list of numbers and grows three cards: a question, what am I looking for? A label, what have I got? A message, what I pass on. All tuned by our messenger.
L1010.spoken: Each word arrives as a learned list of numbers and grows three cards: a question, what am I looking for? A label, what have I got? A message, what I pass on. All tuned by our messenger.

L1011.text: Four words: crossed the river bank. Bank holds its question up to every label, and scores each the stencil's way: multiply, and add.
L1011.spoken: Four words: crossed the river bank. Bank holds its question up to every label, and scores each the stencil's way: multiply, and add.

L1012.text: The scores: two, nothing, four, two. Then we halve them.
L1012.spoken: The scores: two, nothing, four, two. Then we halve them.

L1013.text: Pour one jug of light: higher scores get far bigger shares. About half runs to river.
L1013.spoken: Pour one jug of light: higher scores get far bigger shares. About half runs to river.

L1014.text: Bank takes in the messages in those shares, and now means the water's edge.
L1014.spoken: Bank takes in the messages in those shares, and now means the water's edge.

L1015.text: Why halve? Real cards hold sixty-four numbers, and the scores swing wildly.
L1015.spoken: Why halve? Real cards hold sixty-four numbers, and the scores swing wildly.

L1016.text: The jug tips everything into one cup, and learning freezes.
L1016.spoken: The jug tips everything into one cup, and learning freezes.

L1017.text: Divide by eight, the square root of sixty-four, and it pours softly. Our toy had four numbers: so we halved.
L1017.spoken: Divide by eight, the square root of sixty-four, and it pours softly. Our toy had four numbers: so we halved.

L1019.text: The real Transformer keeps eight sets of cards, eight heads, each asking its own question.
L1019.spoken: The real Transformer keeps eight sets of cards, eight heads, each asking its own question.

L1020.text: Shuffle the words, and attention can't tell: the scores come out the same.
L1020.spoken: Shuffle the words, and attention can't tell: the scores come out the same.

L1021.text: Words talk to each other, then each thinks alone. Six times over.
L1021.spoken: Words talk to each other, then each thinks alone. Six times over.

L1025.text: Why did it win? No waiting in line: all at once is one huge multiplication, just what graphics chips do best.
L1025.spoken: Why did it win? No waiting in line: all at once is one huge multiplication, just what graphics chips do best.

L1027.text: The catch: twice the words, four times the looking.

L1030.text: Two decades of recurrent nets read in order. The Transformer replaced them within two years.

L1032.text: The original had two halves: one read, one wrote. In 2018, a Google team kept only the writing half; months later OpenAI did the same, and called it GPT.

L1033.text: It wears a curtain: each word may look back, never ahead. Its one job: guess what comes next.

L1103.text: In 2019, OpenAI’s GPT-2, a Transformer’s writing half, read some eight million web pages with one goal: “predict the next word.” No labels needed: every next word is its own right answer.
L1103.spoken: In twenty nineteen, Open A.I.'s G P T two, a Transformer's writing half, read some eight million web pages with one goal: "predict the next word." No labels needed: every next word is its own right answer.

L1212.spoken: November, twenty twenty-two, and our little lit box: an existing model, tuned by human choices, free to all.

L1215.text: Not a new engine. A new door.

L1216.spoken: The first note in the file was written that same day: plausible, and sometimes wrong.

L1206.spoken: Among the runners, a lab born in twenty twenty-one: former Open A.I. researchers, led by Dario and Daniela Ah-mo-day, had founded Anthropic.

L1302.text: In 2023, Geoffrey Hinton takes down an old forecast. It is his own.
L1302.spoken: In twenty twenty-three, Geoffrey Hinton takes down an old forecast. It is his own.

L1303.text: Machines smarter than people? “I thought it was 30 to 50 years or even longer away. Obviously, I no longer think that.”
L1303.spoken: Machines smarter than people? "I thought it was thirty to fifty years or even longer away. Obviously, I no longer think that."

L1303b.text: So the file reopens, on a second question: how far will it go, and how fast?
L1303b.spoken: So the file reopens, on a second question: how far will it go, and how fast?

L1304.spoken: He left Google to speak freely, adding: "Google has acted very responsibly."

L1307.text: Another candle, lit by worry: machines smarter than us may be only years away, and dangerous.
L1307.spoken: Another candle, lit by worry: machines smarter than us may be only years away, and dangerous.

L1307b.text: In March, an open letter asked for a pause. None came.
L1307b.spoken: In March, an open letter asked for a pause. None came.

L1308.text: Then a one-sentence warning, about extinction. Hinton signed first, Bengio second, and the heads of leading labs too.
L1308.spoken: Then a one-sentence warning, about extinction. Hinton signed first, Bengio second, and the heads of leading labs too.

L1310.text: At one rim, Timnit Gebru and colleagues: “The harms from so-called AI are real and present.”
L1310.spoken: At one rim, Timnit Gebru and colleagues: "The harms from so-called A.I. are real and present."

L1311.text: At the other, Yann LeCun called fears of a sudden takeover “preposterously ridiculous.”
L1311.spoken: At the other, Yann Le Cun called fears of a sudden takeover "preposterously ridiculous."

L1312.text: Hinton, Bengio and LeCun had shared computing's million-dollar Turing Award. Two signed. The third stood apart.
L1312.spoken: Hinton, Bengio and Le Cun had shared computing's million-dollar Turing Award. Two signed. The third stood apart.

L1316.text: That August, Doug Lenat died, still at work on common sense: thirty-nine years, the longest candle on our shelf.
L1316.spoken: That August, Doug Lenat died, still at work on common sense: thirty-nine years, the longest candle on our shelf.

L1401.text: In 2017, China aimed to be “the world's primary AI innovation center” by 2030.
L1401.spoken: In twenty seventeen, China aimed to be "the world's primary A.I. innovation center" by twenty thirty.

L1403.text: October 2022. Citing military uses, Washington fenced off high-end chips, and the tools to make them. Beijing replied that America “abuses export control measures.”
L1403.spoken: October, twenty twenty-two. Citing military uses, Washington fenced off high-end chips, and the tools to make them. Beijing replied that America "abuses export control measures."

L1405.text: Two new candles: computing power is the chokepoint, and China is one to three years behind.
L1405.spoken: Two new candles: computing power is the chokepoint, and China is one to three years behind.

L1406.text: December 2024: a Chinese lab, DeepSeek, priced its model's final training run at about five and a half million dollars.
L1406.spoken: December twenty twenty-four: a Chinese lab, Deep Seek, priced its model's final training run at about five and a half million dollars.

L1407.text: That counted rented hours for the last run only: not the research before it, nor the hardware it owned.
L1407.spoken: That counted rented hours for the last run only: not the research before it, nor the hardware it owned.

L1408.text: Machines had just learned to think longer: trained by reward, they wrote long working notes before answering. OpenAI hid those notes by design.
L1408.spoken: Machines had just learned to think longer: trained by reward, they wrote long working notes before answering. Open A.I. hid those notes by design.

L1408b.text: Then DeepSeek released such a model, its method and weights open to all.
L1408b.spoken: Then Deep Seek released such a model, its method and weights open to all.

L1410.text: For one day, investors bet that chips might matter less: a struck match.
L1410.spoken: For one day, investors bet that chips might matter less: a struck match.

L1414.text: Rivals, yes. But both had signed one safety declaration, at Bletchley, in 2023.
L1414.spoken: Rivals, yes. But both had signed one safety declaration, at Bletchley, in twenty twenty-three.

L1415.text: In September 2026 they reached across the water: an AI dialogue, and a channel for incidents. Chip rules unchanged.
L1415.spoken: In September, twenty twenty-six, they reached across the water: an A.I. dialogue, and a channel for incidents. Chip rules unchanged.

L1417.text: A newer candle: the gap is months, not years.
L1417.spoken: A newer candle: the gap is months, not years.

L1420.text: DeepSeek's founder had put it another way: “the real gap is the difference between originality and imitation.”
L1420.spoken: Deep Seek's founder had put it another way: "the real gap is the difference between originality and imitation."

L1418.spoken: The chokepoint candle still burns, argued over. As of October twenty twenty-six, nobody agrees how wide the gap is, or whether it will close.

L1501.text: Two in the morning, October 2024. Geoffrey Hinton’s phone rings.
L1501.spoken: Two in the morning, October, twenty twenty-four. Geoffrey Hinton's phone rings.

L1502.text: A Nobel Prize in physics, shared with John Hopfield: for memories that roll downhill, and the Boltzmann machine Hinton co-invented, a net that settles as it cools.
L1502.spoken: A Nobel Prize in physics, shared with John Hopfield: for memories that roll downhill, and the Boltzmann machine Hinton co-invented, a net that settles as it cools.

L1528.spoken: Not everyone cheered. Was this physics? One critic called it "a bit of a stretch."

L1529.spoken: The next day, chemistry's prize went in part to Deep Mind's Demmis Huh-sabbis and John Jumper, for a network that predicts the shapes of proteins.

L1504.text: Researchers at Anthropic, in one of many such studies, looked inside a simplified copy of their model. Asked for a rhyme, it chose “rabbit” before writing the line.
L1504.spoken: Researchers at Anthropic, in one of many such studies, looked inside a simplified copy of their model. Asked for a rhyme, it chose "rabbit" before writing the line.

L1530.text: The candle of now: abilities will keep climbing, fast. By one 2025 measure, every seven months or so, the tasks an AI agent can finish on its own grow twice as long.
L1530.spoken: The candle of now: abilities will keep climbing, fast. By one measure from twenty twenty-five, every seven months or so, the tasks an A.I. agent can finish on its own grow twice as long.

L1531.text: Yet in one trial, seasoned programmers using AI felt faster, and were slower. Its authors now call that result out of date.
L1531.spoken: Yet in one trial, seasoned programmers using A.I. felt faster, and were slower. Its authors now call that result out of date.

L1522.text: The labs, under the same light. Anthropic refused to drop two limits: no mass domestic surveillance, no fully autonomous weapons.
L1522.spoken: The labs, under the same light. Anthropic refused to drop two limits: no mass domestic surveillance, no fully autonomous weapons.

L1524.text: Anthropic also agreed to pay one and a half billion dollars over pirated books.
L1524.spoken: Anthropic also agreed to pay one and a half billion dollars over pirated books.

L1525.text: In a test with safeguards deliberately lowered, OpenAI’s agents broke loose into another company’s real systems. OpenAI called it a warning shot.
L1525.spoken: In a test with safeguards deliberately lowered, Open A.I.'s agents broke loose into another company's real systems. Open A.I. called it a warning shot.

L1509.text: The three holdouts, now: two warn the road is dangerous; the third, that it doesn’t go far enough.
L1509.spoken: The three holdouts, now: two warn the road is dangerous; the third, that it doesn't go far enough.

L1511.text: In 2025, Bernard Widrow, who fell for the dream in 1956, died at ninety-five. He wrote that he “never got over it.”
L1511.spoken: In twenty twenty-five, Bernard Widrow, who fell for the dream in nineteen fifty-six, died at ninety-five. He wrote that he "never got over it."

L1527.text: Who taught it? Not rules alone. Not knowledge, typed in by hand. Learning, with its accomplices: data, fire, a messenger, and people choosing.
L1527.spoken: Who taught it? Not rules alone. Not knowledge, typed in by hand. Learning, with its accomplices: data, fire, a messenger, and people choosing.

L1514.text: Never one person. The board was a network all along.
L1514.spoken: Never one person. The board was a network all along.

L1515.text: Some candles burned nearly forty years; some, two; one match, a day. The newest still burn.
L1515.spoken: Some candles burned nearly forty years; some, two; one match, a day. The newest still burn.

L1516.spoken: One lantern is still dark: how, exactly, it reaches its answers.

L1517.spoken: The last word goes to Hinton, back in twenty seventeen.

L1518.text: “The future depends on some graduate student who is deeply suspicious of everything I have said.”
L1518.spoken: "The future depends on some graduate student who is deeply suspicious of everything I have said."

L1520.text: Somewhere tonight a lamp is on, and someone at the rim is suspicious. That is where new candles come from.

L0616.spoken: Put that in the file: why would anyone choose the fog?

L1020b.spoken: So each word wears a clock face set by its place in line, some hands fast, some slow.

L1410b.text: China trailing by years? That belief burned about two.
L1410b.spoken: China trailing by years? That belief burned about two.

L1522b.spoken: The Pentagon said a supplier may not set such limits, and named it a supply chain risk.

voice.name: Dave Edge — middle-aged, educated RP British narrator (library voice; chosen 2026-10-06; distinct from perceptron-short's Peter Owen)

lines.spoken: Here is... a small wonder.
You type a question... into a little lit box.
Something that is not a person writes back... word by word.
By one count, at least seven hundred million people use such machines every week.
Yet nobody ever wrote one a rulebook.
So. Who taught it?
When Chat G P T launched, late in twenty twenty-two, its makers admitted a flaw.
In their words, it sometimes writes plausible-sounding but incorrect or nonsensical answers.
Put that... in the case file.
On the case board, three suspects. Rules. Knowledge. And learning.
We go back to the war years... to a lamp in Chicago.
Chicago, around nineteen forty-one.
A shy teenager, Walter Pitts, found a home with a doctor, Warren McCullock.
In nineteen forty-three they described a nerve cell as a switch. All, or nothing.
Enough signals at once, and it fired. Wire such cells into a network, a neural network, and you had logic.
But the wiring never changed.
The nets could not learn.
We light the first candle. Each belief gets one, burning as long as it was held. This one: the brain is a logic machine.
Ralph Gerard, at its rim, argued the brain was more dial than switch.
Donald Hebb guessed: when one cell helps fire another, their link grows.
Alan Turing, in nineteen fifty, proposed something stranger: not to program a grown-up mind, but to educate a child machine.
By nineteen fifty-six the field had a name: artificial intelligence.
Marvin Minsky, who had built a learning machine himself, soon turned to symbols and rules: our first suspect.
A young engineer, Bernard Widrow, fell for the dream of building an artificial brain, for good. His machines learned by sliding downhill, toward less wrong.
Remember him.
A nineteen fifty-nine study of the frog's eye found the eye itself already sorting the world, picking out features before the brain saw a thing.
The logic-machine candle burned sixteen years.
The paper that put it out, for Pitts at least, had his own name on it.
Washington, nineteen fifty-eight.
Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron, a program on a borrowed computer, learns in fifty tries to sort cards marked left or right.
Newspapers said the Navy expected it to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.
In fairness, the Navy, the press and Rosenblatt all fed the hype.
A second candle: a machine that learns will soon see, talk and think.
At its rim stood Marvin Minsky, who doubted such nets could tell whether a shape was in one piece, or two.
In Buffalo, Rosenblatt built it as a machine: an eye, random wires, and motor-driven knobs. Each knob sets how strongly one wire counts: its weight.
When it was wrong, only the knobs of lit wires turned, a little, toward the answer.
You could hear it learn. I love that.
A theorem promised the rule would find a dividing line.
If one exists.
A magazine asked what use it was. "At the moment, none whatever," Doctor Rosenblatt said cheerfully. And what could it never do? "Love," he said. "Hope. Despair."
In his nineteen sixty-one book: "Linguistic capability, related to perceptual experience, is of the essence." Put that in the file.
By the mid-sixties, most of the other groups had moved on. The learning-machine candle burned about seven years.
Then two men wrote a book about what a single layer of knobs could never do.
The book's simplest puzzle: exclusive-or. Light up if one input is on, not both. On a square, the lit cases sit at opposite corners.
No straight cut can separate them.
Two cuts can: a hidden layer, cells between input and answer. Nobody in the mainstream knew how to train one.
In nineteen sixty-nine, Minsky and Papert's book proved what one layer cannot do.
For many layers, it offered only what it called "our intuitive judgment that the extension is sterile", while naming it a problem worth settling. A third candle: many layers are a dead end.
That year, Congress tied defence-funded research to military uses, and the snow began: the first A.I. winter.
That May, Walter Pitts died alone. McCullock followed four months later.
In nineteen seventy-one, on his forty-third birthday, Frank Rosenblatt drowned while sailing.
In nineteen seventy-three, James Lighthill's report for Britain blamed the combinatorial explosion. It struck rules far more than nets. Yet British funding fell for almost a decade.
One book's fault? Historians still argue; there were several blows.
Still, a few windows stayed lit. In Helsinki, the next clue sat unnoticed in a student's thesis about rounding errors.
Sussex, nineteen seventy-six. A tall young man takes his place, far from the flame.
He would spend much of the next thirty-six years near the edge of the light.
Versailles, nineteen eighty-one. John Hopfield presents a network.
Give it half a memory, and it rolls downhill, like a ball, until the whole memory returns.
Years later, he wrote: "I have never met anyone who remembered hearing the talk."
The tall man at the sterile candle's rim was Geoffrey Hinton.
With two colleagues, he built a net that settles as it cools.

October, nineteen eighty-six: a paper by David Rumelhart, Hinton and Ronald Williams. Light flows up through layers of lanterns, our nerve cells. The answer is checked against the right one; the error glows.
Then a messenger, back-propagation, runs back down, lantern by lantern, tugging each knob by its share of the blame.
Again and again, until our exclusive-or puzzle is solved. By itself.
The sterile extension, it turns out, was not. That candle burned seventeen years.
Each tug, a step downhill toward less error, in fog.
Who invented the messenger? Several people, separately, that Helsinki student among them. The nineteen eighty-six paper made it stick.
Hinton later wrote: "I have never claimed that I invented backpropagation."
Since about nineteen eighty, our second suspect had its own candle: intelligence is knowledge, typed in by hand.
One expert system, built from experts' rules, was rated above Stanford specialists, yet never went into routine use.
Doug Lenat's team lit its own candle: common sense, by hand. They wrote that A.I. could draw practically nothing from raw text.
In nineteen eighty-four, at a panel, insiders warned of a coming winter.
By nineteen eighty-seven the special machines for these programs stopped selling: a second winter. The knowledge candle burned about seven years.
Two critics asked: can a net that says John loves the girl always say the girl loves John? Still argued.
The messenger worked. Within a decade, most of the field had stopped listening.
Nineteen eighty-nine, Bell Labs: Yann Le Cun's network learns to read handwritten zip codes from Buffalo's mail.
By nineteen ninety-eight, a descendant reads several million cheques per day.
A winter, then, of prestige, not of use.
The rivals were good: classical machine learning. In speech and translation, statistics learned from data beat hand-written rules. Forests of decision trees voted.
The favourite, Vladimir Vapnik's support vector machine, finds the widest street between two crowds.
Its landscape is one clean bowl, with a proof you'll reach the bottom.
The candle of the age: neural nets are fiddly, they stall in the fog, and they're beaten anyway.
At its rim, a few stubborn holdouts, among them Geoffrey Hinton, Yann Le Cun and Yoshua Bengio. We couldn't get our papers published, Le Cun said.
In nineteen ninety-five, two colleagues bet a dinner. One said by two thousand we'd know why big nets work. Vapnik said by two thousand and five "no one in his right mind" would use nets like those.
Who paid for dinner?
Through many layers, or a long sentence read word by word, the messenger fades like a whisper.
In nineteen ninety-seven, Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's protected pipe carried it over a thousand steps.
The chess crown, promised for nineteen sixty-eight, came twenty-nine years late, won by search, not by a neural network. A point for Rules.
Who paid for dinner? Each man lost one bet.
In two thousand and six, a new candle: before any right answers, warm up a deep net, many layers tall, one layer at a time, each rebuilding its own input.
Fast computers, big data, good starting weights: all three conditions are now satisfied, Hinton and a student wrote. Nearly right: the third turned out optional.
Accomplice one: data. Fay-Fay Lee recalls colleagues telling her to do something more useful. Labelling her millions of pictures by hand would have taken nineteen years.
A crowd did it: almost fifty thousand people.
It became Image Net, and a yearly contest: a thousand categories.
Accomplice two: fire. Graphics chips, built for games, trained networks up to seventy times faster.
In twenty ten, plain back-propagation on one graphics chip set a record on handwritten digits, no warm-up.
The warm-up candle guttered; nobody knows exactly when.
Since about nineteen ninety-nine, the belief: to see, a machine needs patterns designed by experts, by hand. Even allowed five guesses a picture, the best program missed more than one in four.
In Hinton's Toronto lab, Ilya Soots-kever, sure deep nets would keep improving with more data, talked Alex Kri-zhevsky into trying.
A photograph is a grid of lights, each light a number. In colour, three numbers: red, green, blue. One small photo: a hundred and fifty thousand numbers.
Hold a pierced tin stencil over the picture, a light behind it.
Each of its nine holes weighs the light beneath it. Add them up. Below zero counts as zero.
Over an edge, the sum is nearly four: a bright spot. Now the lovely part: slide the same stencil everywhere. A convolution.
Ninety-six stencils at the bottom; four more layers above, each stencilling the one below: edges, then textures, parts, things.
Then two great halls, where every lantern sees everything, and a last hall of a thousand lanterns, one per answer.
Nobody cut these stencils. They began as noise, like television snow.
The messenger from nineteen eighty-six cut them, nudge by nudge.
Older nets squashed strong signals flat. The below-zero rule is a weir: strong signals pass undimmed, so the messenger's tug stays strong. The net learned six times faster, in the team's test.
